title: Why an AI productivity gain can raise inflation before it lowers costs
summary: If households anticipate higher future incomes and companies invest ahead of future productivity gains, demand can strengthen before a new technology increases supply. Anna Bartocci, Alessandro Cantelmo, Pietro Cova and Stefania Villa quantify this timing problem in a Bank of Italy occasional paper. Their benchmark is an experiment in which global total factor productivity rises gradually and permanently to 1% above its prior level after five years. The result is a permanent increase in GDP and a temporary increase in inflation. The 1% is an input chosen to compare mechanisms across scenarios. The study supplies neither an estimate of how productive AI has already made firms nor a forecast of what the ECB will do. (pp. 5–7, 14–16).

The world economy in the paper contains the euro area, the United States, China and a residual bloc. Each produces tradable and non-tradable intermediate goods. Their bilateral trading relationships, imports of energy and positions in international financial markets allow a foreign technology shock to affect the prices paid by a European household. Some households can save against anticipated income gains. Others spend their current labour income. Firms face costs when adjusting investment, which delays new capacity even as expected returns rise. The baseline assumes productivity improves in every sector and region. Investment and consumption rise early, and inflation returns toward its target as productive capacity catches up. Appendix Figure A.1 shows why the timing matters: an unexpected, abrupt productivity improvement can instead be disinflationary on impact. (Tables 1–6, Figure 1 and Appendix Figure A.1).

In the broad-based benchmark the euro depreciates against the dollar despite the same productivity improvement in both regions. The euro area is more open to trade and its export response is larger. In the model the exchange rate helps accommodate the change in trade flows. The weaker euro raises the euro price of imported consumer goods, production inputs and energy. It also shifts demand toward domestic producers. A comparison holding exchange rates fixed produces slightly less euro-area inflation, a smaller policy-rate rise and a larger output gain. This identifies the contribution of one transmission channel inside the simulation. It does not establish that a depreciation caused by any piece of technology news would have the same effect. (Figures 1–2 and Appendix Figure A.2).

Which sectors adopt the technology changes the answer. When the authors concentrate the same world productivity gain in non-tradables, used here as a proxy for services, less of it propagates through international trade. Euro-area output, investment, exports, inflation and the interest-rate response all rise by less than in the broad-based experiment. If the United States and China then enjoy larger gains than the euro area, foreign services productivity supplies little additional stimulus to European producers. The euro appreciates against the dollar and renminbi in this case. Cheaper imports cushion domestic inflation and improve purchasing power. Euro-area GDP rises more than in the matching fixed-exchange-rate simulation because the purchasing-power gain outweighs the drag on exports. The assumption about which sectors gain is therefore essential to interpreting even the sign of the currency move. (Figures 2–4 and Appendix Figure A.2).

Employment anxiety introduces a separate demand channel. In the paper it is a change in households’ willingness to spend, calibrated so consumption initially stays flat. The model does not simulate AI replacing identifiable jobs. With more saving, consumption and investment expand less, and the increases in policy rates and inflation become smaller. Rate paths throughout are generated by the same calibrated reaction rule across regions. A difference in the simulated ECB and US paths is an outcome of the shocks and structures fed into that rule. It supplies no evidence that either institution has adopted a new policy preference. (Figures 2 and 5).

Financial markets can reverse a trade-led currency response. In a further experiment, stronger demand for US assets is represented by a financial shock calibrated to appreciate the dollar by 1%. This offsets some of the euro appreciation generated by asymmetric productivity gains and modestly increases euro-area inflation through import prices. The authors also examine weaker foreign demand for dollar bonds. In Appendix Figure A.3 the desired ratio of those holdings to GDP falls by one percentage point, weakening the dollar further against the euro with comparatively small effects on euro-area activity. For an investor, the observed currency move is consequently a poor stand-alone measure of AI’s productivity effect. It can convey information about the sector producing the gains, the country accumulating new capital, or the kind of dollar asset investors want to hold. (Figure 6 and Appendix Figure A.3).

questions.question: Did investment spending turn before measured productive capacity?
questions.detail: Match adoption surveys and corporate investment announcements to actual equipment spending, capacity utilisation, output per hour and services prices. A rise in orders and investment ahead of productivity would fit the anticipated transition. An immediate gain in output per input with little change in demand would instead resemble the paper’s abrupt-shock case. Distinguish the timing of announcements from installed equipment. Consult national statistical agencies’ productivity releases, investment surveys and listed companies’ capital-spending disclosures on the same dates.

questions.question: Are AI gains appearing in tradable production or locally supplied services?
questions.detail: Compare sector productivity with import content, exports and bilateral demand. Check whether the larger adopters are selling into external markets or primarily supplying domestic customers. The same global productivity increment produces much smaller European spillovers when foreign gains are concentrated in non-tradables. A services label alone cannot determine tradability, particularly for digital services. Input-output tables and sector-level national accounts can distinguish a measured gain in local services from one transmitted through cross-border supply chains.

questions.question: Did a currency move reflect expected productivity or increased demand for US assets?
questions.detail: Place euro-dollar changes alongside relative rate expectations, sectoral equity returns, cross-border flows into US corporate assets and foreign demand for Treasuries. Ports, export orders and import prices provide a slower-moving check on the trade channel. The paper gives the capital-flow shock a chosen size, so an estimate for an actual market move requires independent evidence on the associated financial flows. Balance-of-payments data and official securities-holdings statistics would help identify which assets attracted investors.
